title: Mitigating Capability Degradation in LLM Self-Improvement via Representation Geometry Regularization

paper.title: Mitigating Capability Degradation in LLM Self-Improvement via Representation Geometry Regularization
paper.abstract:
Abstract On-Policy Self-distillation is a self-improvement paradigm that enables large language models (LLMs) to improve their capabilities by leveraging the same model as both teacher and student under different conditioning contexts.
However, we find that OPSD methods can progressively degrade previously acquired capabilities: queries that are correctly responded at earlier training stages may become incorrectly responded as optimization proceeds, even the overall performance continues to improve. Further analysis reveals that this degradation coincides with a deterioration of the geometry of hidden representations, characterized by reduced intra-cluster compactness and diminished inter-cluster separation. Motivated by this observation, we propose Representation Geometry Regularization (RGR), which preserves representation geometry during post-training by encouraging compactness within cluster and separation across cluster. RGR can be seamlessly integrated into existing OPSD methods without altering their core optimization procedures. Extensive experiments on multiple OPSD methods and benchmarks show that RGR generally alleviates capability degradation while retaining capability improvements. Our code is available in https://github.com/supermachinelearner/RGR

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: (a) The capability degradation ratio of existing methods; (b) Although the overall performance improves during training, some problems that were previously responded correctly become incorrectly answered as optimization progresses. On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , is a self-improvement paradigm for the post-training of large language models (LLMs) ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) , which enables LLMs to improve their capabilities through self-knowledge distillation. Unlike conventional knowledge distillation ( Hinton et al., 2015 ; Sanh et al., 2019 ) , which relies on a separately trained teacher, OPSD uses the same LLM as both teacher and student under different conditioning contexts. Specifically, the student model generates responses to the original query, while teacher model, which share the same parameters with the student model, conditioned on additional privileged information (e.g., verified reasoning traces) to provide supervision for these generated responses. Although recent studies ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) have empirically demonstrated that optimizing the LLM with OPSD can outperform conventional post-training methods such as SFT ( Wei et al., 2021 ) and GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , benefiting from the dense and fine-grained token-level supervision of OPSD. We observe a progressive reasoning capability degradation phenomenon during self-improvement in existing OPSD methods. As shown in Figure 1 (b), a query that is responded correctly at earlier training stages gradually becomes incorrectly responded as training proceeds, even as overall performance continues to improve. Furthermore, we examine several representative OPSD methods and find that this phenomenon consistently occurs across these methods, albeit to varying degrees, as it is shown in Figure 1 (a). Such degradation may undermine the stability of self-improvement. To better understand this phenomenon, we conduct further analysis, and the results reveal that this capability degradation is accompanied by a progressive deterioration in the geometry of hidden representations. When a query is answered correctly at earlier stages of training, the hidden representations of its generated responses exhibit a relatively well-structured clustering pattern, characterized by larger inter-cluster distances and clearer cluster boundaries. As training proceeds and the response to the same query gradually becomes incorrect, the relative distances between clusters shrink and the cluster boundaries become increasingly indistinct. This observation suggests that preserving the geometric structure of the representation space may be important for maintaining previously acquired capabilities during self-improvement. Based on this finding, we theoretically show that preserving intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster separation in the hidden representation space helps maintain the capabilities that the LLM has already acquired. Based on this theoretical insight, we develop Representation Geometry Regularization (RGR), which constrains the evolution of hidden representations during self-improvement. RGR incorporates two geometry-preserving constraints called intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster separation into the OPSD methods, enabling the model to improve targeted capabilities while mitigating the degradation of previously acquired ones. Experiments across four existing SD models and three widely used benchmarks show that RGR substantially reduces correct-to-incorrect transitions during training while retaining its self-improvement gains. In summary, our contributions are summarized as follows: • We uncover an overlooked failure mode, where OPSD methods can degrade previously acquired capabilities, causing previously correct predictions to become incorrect. • We identify representation geometry distortion as a key factor underlying this degradation, and theoretically characterize the importance of hidden representation geometry for prediction stability. • We propose RGR, which incorporates geometry-preserving constraints into OPSD methods to enable self-improvement while reducing capability degradation.

sections.heading: 2 Related works
sections.text: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables LLMs to improve their capabilities without requiring an external model as a teacher. Recently, it has attracted significant attention as a promising paradigm for scalable and efficient LLM self-improvement. Based on how self-teacher signals are constructed and how external feedback is incorporated, we organize existing OPSD methods into privileged-information-driven methods and external-feedback-driven methods.The privileged-information-driven methods construct self-teacher signals using additional privileged information that is unavailable to the student policy at inference time. As a representative method, OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) uses the same model to construct self-teacher signals and optimize the student policy under different conditioning contexts: the self-teacher signals are constructed from both the question and a verified reasoning trace, whereas the student policy is conditioned only on the question. The external-feedback-driven methods retain the self-teacher structure while incorporating environmental feedback, verification results, or outcome rewards to construct the supervision for policy updating. Within this category, feedback can be used to construct distillation targets, select training objectives, or modulate token-level advantages. SDPO ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) conditions the current model on textual or reward-derived feedback to form a self-teacher, whose next-token predictions serve as distillation targets for the student policy. SRPO ( Li et al., 2026 ) routes successful trajectories to reward-driven GRPO updates and failed trajectories to entropy-weighted, token-level self-distillation against a feedback-conditioned teacher distribution. RLSD ( Yang et al., 2026 ) uses verifiable outcomes to determine the direction of policy updates and token-level teacher–student discrepancies to modulate their magnitude, integrating self-distillation into reward-driven learning.

sections.heading: 3 Preliminaries
sections.text: Given a query q q , an LLM π θ \pi_{\theta} typically generates a response y = ( y 1 , … , y T ) y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}) according to y t ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ q , y < t ) y_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,y_{<t}) , where y < t = ( y 1 , … , y t − 1 ) y_{<t}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{t-1}) denotes the previously generated tokens. OPSD methods improve the LLM by using the same model under different conditioning contexts as the teacher and student to conduct knowledge distillation. Specifically, the student is designed to generate an on-policy response based only on the original query, like the LLM, i.e. , y ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ q ) y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q) . sections.heading: 4.1 Progressive Capability Degradation
sections.text: Figure 2: Hidden-state representations and response correctness across training epochs. The query is answered correctly at epochs 25 and 50, but incorrectly at epoch 75. As discussed previously, although OPSD methods continuously improve the overall performance in the training, some queries that are correctly responded at earlier training stages become incorrectly responded as training proceeds. To better understand this phenomenon, for a fixed query, we generate a response and visualize the hidden representations corresponding to the generated response every 25 training epochs. We observe that changes in the geometry of the hidden representations consistently coincide with changes in response correctness. As illustrated in Figure. 2 , when the model generates a correct response at an earlier training stage (Epoch 25), the corresponding hidden representations exhibit a relatively structured geometric organization, with clearly distinguishable clusters and relatively large distances between clusters. As training proceeds and the response becomes incorrect, the relative distances between clusters gradually decrease, while the boundaries between clusters become increasingly indistinct (Epoch 75). We hypothesize that as a query transitions from being correctly to incorrectly responded, the reasoning process in the generated response gradually becomes less coherent. When the query is answered correctly, the reasoning tends to exhibit a clear and consistent logical structure, which is reflected in the hidden representation space as distinct and well-separated clusters corresponding to different reasoning patterns. As the reasoning becomes increasingly disorganized, these patterns become less distinguishable, causing the corresponding representations to become more entangled and eventually leading to an incorrect response. Interestingly, this phenomenon is consistently observed in existing OPSD methods, such as OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , SDPO ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) , RLSD ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , SRPO ( Li et al., 2026 ) . These observations suggest a strong connection between the geometry of the hidden representation and the stability of the model’s acquired capabilities during self-improvement.

sections.heading: 5 Methodology
sections.text: As discussed previously, we observe that increasingly blurred boundaries between hidden representation clusters coincide with the progressive degradation of model capabilities during OPSD training. Motivated by this observation, we propose Representation Geometry Regularization (RGR) to preserve clear boundaries between hidden representation clusters. To achieve this goal, we consider two complementary geometric properties: (1) intra-cluster compactness, where representations within each cluster remain sufficiently compact, and (2) inter-cluster separation, where different clusters maintain sufficient separation from each other. In the following, we discuss how to preserve the two properties in detail and derive the corresponding regularization objectives.

sections.heading: 5.1 Intra-cluster compactness
sections.text: According to previous works , the intra-cluster compactness of hidden representations can be evaluated by the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) ( Lloyd, 1982 ) , defined as the sum of squared distances between each hidden representation and the center of its corresponding cluster. However, directly minimizing WCSS may lead to excessive compactness within each cluster. In the extreme case, hidden representations within the same cluster may become overly similar, reducing the discriminative information encoded in the representation space. Therefore, we introduce the teacher model as a reference and encourage the WCSS of the student representations within each cluster to remain close to that of the teacher representations. (11) In addition to representation geometry, recent studies ( Jin et al., 2026 ) on on-policy distillation have highlighted the importance of controlling the entropy of the model output distribution during optimization,which motivates us to explicitly incorporate an entropy-related objective into the optimization process. Accordingly, we jointly preserve the hidden representation geometry and regulate the output distribution entropy during OPSD optimization. Combining the original OPSD objective with the geometry-preserving and entropy-related objectives, we formulate the overall training objective as ℒ = ℒ OPSD + α ​ ℒ geo + β ​ ℒ ent , \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}+\alpha\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geo}}+\beta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ent}}, (12) where ℒ OPSD \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}} denotes the original on-policy self-distillation objective, ℒ geo \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geo}} denotes the proposed geometry-preserving regularization, and ℒ ent = ‖ 𝐇 ⊤ ​ 𝐇 − 𝐇 ref ⊤ ​ 𝐇 ref ‖ F 2 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ent}}=\left\|\mathbf{H}^{\top}\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{ref}}^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{ref}}\right\|_{F}^{2} denotes the entropy-related objective. The coefficients α \alpha and β \beta control the contributions of the geometry-preserving and entropy-related terms, respectively.

sections.heading: 6 EXEPERIMENT
sections.text: In this section, we conduct experiments to evaluate the performance of RGR. We aim to answer the following research questions: (1) Is RGR effective for improving the performance of self distillation (RQ1)? (2) How do different components of RGR contribute to the performance gains (RQ2)? (3) Can RGR alleviate the degradation of previously acquired capabilities during OPSD optimization, and how does it affect the evolution of hidden representations (RQ3)? (4) Can RGR generalize to task-transfer settings and alleviate the degradation of previously acquired capabilities when learning new tasks (RQ4)?

sections.heading: Datasets.
sections.text: Following the dataset setup of OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , we sample up to 30K problem-solution pairs containing chain-of-thought reasoning from the mathematical reasoning subset of OpenThoughts ( Guha et al., ) for model training.. We conduct evaluation on three representative benchmarks: AIME 2024 ( Zhang and Math-AI, 2024 ) , AIME 2025 ( Zhang and Math-AI, 2025 ) , and HMMT 2025 ( Balunovic et al., 2026 ) . AIME 2024 consists of problems from the 2024 American Invitational Mathematics Examination, covering diverse areas of high-school mathematics. AIME 2025 consists of problems from the 2025 American Invitational Mathematics Examination. HMMT 2025 consists of problems from the Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament, covering algebra, combinatorics, geometry, and number theory.

sections.heading: Baseline.
sections.text: To assess the effectiveness of RGR, we integrate it into four representative self-distillation methods, namely, OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , SDPO ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) , SRPO ( Li et al., 2026 ) , and RLSD ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and compare each RGR-enhanced method with its original counterpart. These methods differ in how they optimize the self-distillation objective. Specifically, OPSD employs forward KL divergence ( Kullback and Leibler, 1951 ) , with the policy update constrained by token-level KL clipping; SDPO uses Jensen–Shannon divergence ( Lin, 1991 ) to align the student with the teacher; SRPO routes successful responses to reward-based reinforcement and failed responses to self-distillation; and RLSD uses environment-derived rewards to determine the direction of policy updates, while reweighting token-level advantages according to the teacher–student log-probability gap to modulate the update magnitude.

sections.heading: ImplementationDetails.
sections.text: Our experiments are conducted on two foundation LLMs: Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , with thinking mode enabled throughout training and validation. All experiments are performed on four NVIDIA A40 GPUs. All methods use LoRA ( Hu et al., 2021 ) with a rank of 64 and a scaling factor of 128, with the learning rate set to 5 × \times 10 − 6 10^{-6} . The teacher model remains frozen throughout training. For our method, we fix the parameter α \alpha in Eq.( 12 ) at 2.5 × 10 − 2 2.5\times 10^{-2} and the parameter β \beta in Eq.( 12 ) at 5 × 10 − 2 5\times 10^{-2} across all benchmarks.

sections.heading: 6.4 Training Dynamics Visualization (RQ3)
sections.text: Effect of RGR on mitigating progressive capability degradation. To evaluate whether RGR alleviates progressive capability degradation, we compare the ratio of queries that transition from correct to incorrect responses before and after incorporating RGR into different OPSD variants. As shown in Figure 3 , adding RGR consistently reduces the degradation ratio across all evaluated methods. Specifically, RGR eliminates the degradation in OPSD and reduces the degradation ratios of SDPO, RLSD, and SRPO by 14.28%, 7.15%, and 21.43%, respectively. These results demonstrate that RGR not only improves self-improvement performance but also helps preserve previously acquired capabilities by maintaining a more stable hidden representation geometry during optimization. Representation geometry analysis. To further understand how RGR alleviates progressive capability degradation, we visualize the hidden representations of responses corresponding to the degraded queries. Specifically, we select queries that are initially responded correctly but become incorrectly responded during optimization, and compare the representation geometry before and after incorporating RGR. As shown in Figure 4 , without RGR, the hidden representations gradually lose their geometric structure, exhibiting reduced inter-cluster center separation and less distinguishable cluster boundaries when the response changes from correct to incorrect. In contrast, RGR maintains more compact clusters with clearer boundaries in most cases. These results are consistent with our theoretical analysis and demonstrate that preserving representation geometry helps stabilize the evolution of hidden representations during OPSD training. sections.heading: 6.5 Cross-Task Forgetting Study (RQ4)
sections.text: To further investigate whether RGR can mitigate capability degradation beyond the original task, we conduct a cross-task forgetting experiment. We first post-train a model on OpenThoughts to acquire mathematical problem-solving capabilities, and evaluate the model on AIME24 to measure performance. Then we continue post-training it on a tool-use dataset ( Tang et al., 2023 ) , after convergence, we evaluate the model again on AIME24 to measure the performance after tool-use training. We apply this setting to OPSD, SDPO, RLSD, and SRPO, and compare their performance before and after training on the tool-use dataset, as shown in Table 3 . From Table 3 , we can observe that: (1) Sequential training on a new task leads to forgetting of previously acquired capabilities. After tool-use training, all four methods exhibit performance degradation on AIME24, consistent with previous studies of catastrophic forgetting in continual fine-tuning of LLMs ( Luo et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . (2) RGR generally alleviates cross-task forgetting. RGR reduces the forgetting gap for OPSD, SDPO, and SRPO, with particularly notable improvements for SDPO (5.28 → \rightarrow 1.94) and SRPO (3.06 → \rightarrow 1.11). This suggests that preserving representation geometry during subsequent optimization can help retain previously acquired capabilities. (3) The effectiveness of RGR depends on the underlying post-training method. For RLSD, the forgetting gap slightly increases from 3.05 to 3.39 after introducing RGR, suggesting that the effect of representation geometry preservation may vary across different optimization dynamics. Nevertheless, RGR reduces forgetting for three of the four methods, supporting its broader applicability to sequential post-training.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we identify and investigate the progressive capability degradation phenomenon in on-policy self-distillation, where LLM may lose previously acquired capabilities during self-improvement despite overall performance improvements. Through empirical analysis and theoretical investigation, we reveal that this degradation is associated with the deterioration of hidden representation geometry, characterized by reduced intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster center separation. Based on these findings, we propose Representation Geometry Regularization (RGR), a general regularization framework that preserves intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster center separation during OPSD optimization. Extensive experiments across multiple OPSD variants and mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RGR effectively reduces correct-to-incorrect transitions while maintaining the self-improvement capability of OPSD. Future work will explore more adaptive strategies for preserving representation geometry and extending the proposed framework to broader model optimization paradigms beyond self-distillation.

Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence Affiliation: Jilin University Affiliation: China Email: longting@jlu.edu.cn Abstract On-Policy Self-distillation is a self-improvement paradigm that enables large language models (LLMs) to improve their capabilities by leveraging the same model as both teacher and student under different conditioning contexts. However, we find that OPSD methods can progressively degrade previously acquired capabilities: queries that are correctly responded at earlier training stages may become incorrectly responded as optimization proceeds, even the overall performance continues to improve. Further analysis reveals that this degradation coincides with a deterioration of the geometry of hidden representations, characterized by reduced intra-cluster compactness and diminished inter-cluster separation. Motivated by this observation, we propose Representation Geometry Regularization (RGR), which preserves representation geometry during post-training by encouraging compactness within cluster and separation across cluster. RGR can be seamlessly integrated into existing OPSD methods without altering their core optimization procedures. Extensive experiments on multiple OPSD methods and benchmarks show that RGR generally alleviates capability degradation while retaining capability improvements. Our code is available in https://github.com/supermachinelearner/RGR 1 Introduction Figure 1: (a) The capability degradation ratio of existing methods; (b) Although the overall performance improves during training, some problems that were previously responded correctly become incorrectly answered as optimization progresses. On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , is a self-improvement paradigm for the post-training of large language models (LLMs) ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) , which enables LLMs to improve their capabilities through self-knowledge distillation. Unlike conventional knowledge distillation ( Hinton et al., 2015 ; Sanh et al., 2019 ) , which relies on a separately trained teacher, OPSD uses the same LLM as both teacher and student under different conditioning contexts. Specifically, the student model generates responses to the original query, while teacher model, which share the same parameters with the student model, conditioned on additional privileged information (e.g., verified reasoning traces) to provide supervision for these generated responses. Although recent studies ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) have empirically demonstrated that optimizing the LLM with OPSD can outperform conventional post-training methods such as SFT ( Wei et al., 2021 ) and GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , benefiting from the dense and fine-grained token-level supervision of OPSD. We observe a progressive reasoning capability degradation phenomenon during self-improvement in existing OPSD methods. As shown in Figure 1 (b), a query that is responded correctly at earlier training stages gradually becomes incorrectly responded as training proceeds, even as overall performance continues to improve. Furthermore, we examine several representative OPSD methods and find that this phenomenon consistently occurs across these methods, albeit to varying degrees, as it is shown in Figure 1 (a). Such degradation may undermine the stability of self-improvement. To better understand this phenomenon, we conduct further analysis, and the results reveal that this capability degradation is accompanied by a progressive deterioration in the geometry of hidden representations. When a query is answered correctly at earlier stages of training, the hidden representations of its generated responses exhibit a relatively well-structured clustering pattern, characterized by larger inter-cluster distances and clearer cluster boundaries. As training proceeds and the response to the same query gradually becomes incorrect, the relative distances between clusters shrink and the cluster boundaries become increasingly indistinct. This observation suggests that preserving the geometric structure of the representation space may be important for maintaining previously acquired capabilities during self-improvement. Based on this finding, we theoretically show that preserving intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster separation in the hidden representation space helps maintain the capabilities that the LLM has already acquired. Based on this theoretical insight, we develop Representation Geometry Regularization (RGR), which constrains the evolution of hidden representations during self-improvement. RGR incorporates two geometry-preserving constraints called intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster separation into the OPSD methods, enabling the model to improve targeted capabilities while mitigating the degradation of previously acquired ones. Experiments across four existing SD models and three widely used benchmarks show that RGR substantially reduces correct-to-incorrect transitions during training while retaining its self-improvement gains. In summary, our contributions are summarized as follows: • We uncover an overlooked failure mode, where OPSD methods can degrade previously acquired capabilities, causing previously correct predictions to become incorrect. • We identify representation geometry distortion as a key factor underlying this degradation, and theoretically characterize the importance of hidden representation geometry for prediction stability. • We propose RGR, which incorporates geometry-preserving constraints into OPSD methods to enable self-improvement while reducing capability degradation. 2 Related works On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables LLMs to improve their capabilities without requiring an external model as a teacher. Recently, it has attracted significant attention as a promising paradigm for scalable and efficient LLM self-improvement. Based on how self-teacher signals are constructed and how external feedback is incorporated, we organize existing OPSD methods into privileged-information-driven methods and external-feedback-driven methods.The privileged-information-driven methods construct self-teacher signals using additional privileged information that is unavailable to the student policy at inference time. As a representative method, OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) uses the same model to construct self-teacher signals and optimize the student policy under different conditioning contexts: the self-teacher signals are constructed from both the question and a verified reasoning trace, whereas the student policy is conditioned only on the question. The external-feedback-driven methods retain the self-teacher structure while incorporating environmental feedback, verification results, or outcome rewards to construct the supervision for policy updating. Within this category, feedback can be used to construct distillation targets, select training objectives, or modulate token-level advantages. SDPO ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) conditions the current model on textual or reward-derived feedback to form a self-teacher, whose next-token predictions serve as distillation targets for the student policy. SRPO ( Li et al., 2026 ) routes successful trajectories to reward-driven GRPO updates and failed trajectories to entropy-weighted, token-level self-distillation against a feedback-conditioned teacher distribution. RLSD ( Yang et al., 2026 ) uses verifiable outcomes to determine the direction of policy updates and token-level teacher–student discrepancies to modulate their magnitude, integrating self-distillation into reward-driven learning. 3 Preliminaries Given a query q q , an LLM π θ \pi_{\theta} typically generates a response y = ( y 1 , … , y T ) y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}) according to y t ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ q , y < t ) y_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,y_{<t}) , where y < t = ( y 1 , … , y t − 1 ) y_{<t}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{t-1}) denotes the previously generated tokens. The query is answered correctly at epochs 25 and 50, but incorrectly at epoch 75. As discussed previously, although OPSD methods continuously improve the overall performance in the training, some queries that are correctly responded at earlier training stages become incorrectly responded as training proceeds. To better understand this phenomenon, for a fixed query, we generate a response and visualize the hidden representations corresponding to the generated response every 25 training epochs. We observe that changes in the geometry of the hidden representations consistently coincide with changes in response correctness. As illustrated in Figure. 2 , when the model generates a correct response at an earlier training stage (Epoch 25), the corresponding hidden representations exhibit a relatively structured geometric organization, with clearly distinguishable clusters and relatively large distances between clusters. As training proceeds and the response becomes incorrect, the relative distances between clusters gradually decrease, while the boundaries between clusters become increasingly indistinct (Epoch 75). We hypothesize that as a query transitions from being correctly to incorrectly responded, the reasoning process in the generated response gradually becomes less coherent. When the query is answered correctly, the reasoning tends to exhibit a clear and consistent logical structure, which is reflected in the hidden representation space as distinct and well-separated clusters corresponding to different reasoning patterns. As the reasoning becomes increasingly disorganized, these patterns become less distinguishable, causing the corresponding representations to become more entangled and eventually leading to an incorrect response. Interestingly, this phenomenon is consistently observed in existing OPSD methods, such as OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , SDPO ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) , RLSD ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , SRPO ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Motivated by this observation, we propose Representation Geometry Regularization (RGR) to preserve clear boundaries between hidden representation clusters. To achieve this goal, we consider two complementary geometric properties: (1) intra-cluster compactness, where representations within each cluster remain sufficiently compact, and (2) inter-cluster separation, where different clusters maintain sufficient separation from each other. In the extreme case, hidden representations within the same cluster may become overly similar, reducing the discriminative information encoded in the representation space. (2) How do different components of RGR contribute to the performance gains (RQ2)? (3) Can RGR alleviate the degradation of previously acquired capabilities during OPSD optimization, and how does it affect the evolution of hidden representations (RQ3)? Following the dataset setup of OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , we sample up to 30K problem-solution pairs containing chain-of-thought reasoning from the mathematical reasoning subset of OpenThoughts ( Guha et al., ) for model training.. We conduct evaluation on three representative benchmarks: AIME 2024 ( Zhang and Math-AI, 2024 ) , AIME 2025 ( Zhang and Math-AI, 2025 ) , and HMMT 2025 ( Balunovic et al., 2026 ) . Nevertheless, RGR reduces forgetting for three of the four methods, supporting its broader applicability to sequential post-training. 7 Conclusion In this work, we identify and investigate the progressive capability degradation phenomenon in on-policy self-distillation, where LLM may lose previously acquired capabilities during self-improvement despite overall performance improvements. Through empirical analysis and theoretical investigation, we reveal that this degradation is associated with the deterioration of hidden representation geometry, characterized by reduced intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster center separation. Based on these findings, we propose Representation Geometry Regularization (RGR), a general regularization framework that preserves intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster center separation during OPSD optimization. Extensive experiments across multiple OPSD variants and mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RGR effectively reduces correct-to-incorrect transitions while maintaining the self-improvement capability of OPSD. Future work will explore more adaptive strategies for preserving representation geometry and extending the proposed framework to broader model optimization paradigms beyond self-distillation.
